name: Hall

label: lem:preferred
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Hall deficiency with prescribed coverage

title: Proof
body_md:
Any matching covers at most $|N_B(S)|$ vertices of $S$, so it leaves
at least $|S|-|N_B(S)|$ vertices of $Q_0$ uncovered. This proves the
lower bound. Notice that $\delta\ge0$, since $S=\varnothing$ is
permitted in~\eqref{eq:preferreddef}.

To attain the bound without yet requiring saturation of $L$, take
$B[L\cup Q_0]$ and add $\delta$ new vertices to the part $L$, each
adjacent to every vertex of $Q_0$. For every nonempty
$S\subseteq Q_0$, its new neighborhood has size
$|N_B(S)|+\delta\ge |S|$. Hall's theorem gives a matching saturating
$Q_0$. Deleting the edges incident with the new vertices gives a
matching $J$ in $B[L\cup Q_0]$ leaving at most $\delta$ vertices
of $Q_0$ uncovered, and hence exactly $\delta$ by the lower bound.

Regard $J$ as a matching of $B$. If it does not saturate $L$, compare
it with a matching $K$ that does. The symmetric difference
$J\triangle K=(J\setminus K)\cup(K\setminus J)$ consists of paths
and even cycles whose edges alternate between the two matchings.
Since $|K|>|J|$, some path has one more edge of $K$ than of $J$;
its end-vertices are exposed by $J$. Exchanging the edges along this
path increases $|J|$ by one and preserves every vertex already
covered by $J$. Repeat until $L$ is saturated. The final matching
still covers all the previously covered vertices of $Q_0$, so it leaves at most $\delta$ vertices of $Q_0$ uncovered. By the lower bound, it leaves at least $\delta$ vertices of $Q_0$ uncovered. It therefore has the required properties.

label: thm:GE
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Gallai--Edmonds

label: lem:pairing
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Pairing inequality

title: Proof
body_md:
The set $W$ is independent, since an edge joining two exposed
vertices could be added to $M$. Order the matching edges as
$e_1,\ldots,e_s$ and regard each of them as a pair of vertices.
For each specified pair $P_i$, let $j(i)$ be the first index such
that $e_G(P_i,V(e_{j(i)}))$ is odd. Insert $P_i$ immediately after
$e_{j(i)}$, in any order if several pairs have the same index.
All earlier matching pairs have an even number of edges to $P_i$,
and the matching pair at index $j(i)$ has an odd number. Since
there are no edges within $W$, the total number of edges from $P_i$
to the preceding vertices is odd. Pair the remaining vertices of
$W$ arbitrarily and append these pairs; their number is even because
$n-2s-2q$ is even.

Process the resulting ordered partition of $V(G)$ into pairs.
At each step place one vertex of the current pair in each part,
choosing the placement with more edges crossing to earlier vertices.
If $b$ edges join the current pair to earlier vertices, the two
placements have crossing counts summing to $b$, so the better
placement contributes at least $\left\lceil b/2\right\rceil$ of these edges.
Any edge within the pair crosses in either placement.

For a matching pair, the newly counted edges number $b+1$, and
at least $b/2+1=(b+1)/2+1/2$ of them cross. For a specified pair
$P_i$, there is no internal edge and $b$ is odd, so at least
$(b+1)/2$ of its $b$ newly counted edges cross. Every other pair
contributes at least half its newly counted edges. Each edge of
$G$ is counted exactly once. Summing the gains of $1/2$ from the
$s$ matching pairs and $q$ specified pairs proves~\eqref{eq:pairbound}.
Both parts contain one vertex from every pair, so they have equal size.

label: lem:deficiency
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Degree-deficiency bound

label: eq:internaldef
title: Proof
body_md:
First take $T\in\mathcal E$ and put $u=|V(T)|$. Since its internal degrees
are even and $k$ is odd,
$d_T(v)\le\min\{k-1,u-1\}$ for every $v\in V(T)$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:internaldef}
k|V(T)|-2e(T)
\ge u\bigl(k-\min\{k-1,u-1\}\bigr)\ge k.
\end{equation}
Indeed, if $u\ge k$, the middle expression is at least $u\ge k$;
if $1\le u\le k$, it is at least
$u(k-u+1)=k+(u-1)(k-u)\ge k$.

For any $\mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal E$, let
$U=\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal X}V(T)$ and $Z=N_B(\mathcal X)\subseteq A$.
The components in $\mathcal X$ have no edges to one another, and every
edge leaving $U$ ends in $Z$: there are no edges from $D$ to $R$,
and different components of $G[D]$ have no edges between them.
Therefore
\begin{align}
\Phi_k(G)
&\ge\sum_{v\in U}\bigl(k-d_G(v)\bigr)\notag\\
&=\sum_{T\in\mathcal X}\bigl(k|V(T)|-2e(T)\bigr)-e_G(U,Z)\notag\\
&\ge k|\mathcal X|-k|Z|
 =k\bigl(|\mathcal X|-|N_B(\mathcal X)|\bigr).\label{eq:boundarycount}
\end{align}
The first inequality uses nonnegativity of the degree deficiencies;
the last uses~\eqref{eq:internaldef} and
$e_G(U,Z)\le\sum_{z\in Z}d_G(z)\le k|Z|$.
Taking the maximum over $\mathcal X\subseteq\mathcal E$ proves~\eqref{eq:keydef}.

label: prop:structural
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a matching $J$ of $B$ saturating $A$ and leaving exactly
$t=t(G)$ components of $\mathcal E$ uncovered, as guaranteed by
Lemma~\ref{lem:preferred}. Let $g$ be the number of components of
$\mathcal O$ not covered by $J$.

Lift $J$ to a maximum matching $M$ of $G$ as described after
Theorem~\ref{thm:GE}. In every component $T\in\mathcal O$ not covered
by $J$, choose a vertex $w_T$ of odd internal degree and use a
perfect matching of $T-w_T$. In every uncovered component of
$\mathcal E$, expose an arbitrary vertex. The set $W$ of vertices exposed
by $M$ consequently contains one vertex from each uncovered
component and no other vertices. Put $s=|M|$, and let $W_{\mathcal O}$
be the exposed vertices chosen in components of $\mathcal O$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counts}
|W_{\mathcal O}|=g,\qquad |W\setminus W_{\mathcal O}|=t,\qquad n=2s+g+t.
\end{equation}

We claim that any pair $\{w,w'\}$ with $w\in W_{\mathcal O}$ and
$w'\in W\setminus\{w\}$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:oddadjacency}.
Let $T$ be the component containing $w$. The matching edges inside
$T$ cover $T-w$. As $d_T(w)$ is odd, at least one of those matching
edges inside $T$, say $xy$, has exactly one end-vertex adjacent to $w$; otherwise counting the neighbors of $w$ in these pairs would give an even degree. The vertex $w'$ is in a different component of $G[D]$, and hence is adjacent to neither $x$ nor $y$. Thus $e_G(\{w,w'\},\{x,y\})=1,$ which proves the claim.

If $g$ is even, pair all vertices of $W_{\mathcal O}$ among themselves.
If $g$ is odd, then~\eqref{eq:counts} and the evenness of $n$ imply
that $t$ is odd, so $t\ge1$. Pair one vertex of $W_{\mathcal O}$ with
one vertex of $W\setminus W_{\mathcal O}$, and pair the remaining vertices
of $W_{\mathcal O}$ among themselves. In either case, this gives
$q=\left\lceil g/2\right\rceil$ disjoint pairs satisfying~\eqref{eq:oddadjacency}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:pairing} now yields
\[
\operatorname{bis}(G)\ge\frac m2+\frac{s+q}{2}
\ge\frac m2+\frac{s}{2}+\frac g4
=\frac m2+\frac{n-t}{4},
\]
as required.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $k$ is odd. We may
assume that $n$ is even: otherwise, add one isolated vertex, apply
the even-order assertion, and delete that vertex from the resulting
bisection. This changes neither $m$ nor the maximum-degree bound
and loses no crossing edges.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:deficiency} and Proposition~\ref{prop:structural},
\[
\operatorname{bis}(G)\ge\frac m2+\frac{n-t(G)}4
\ge\frac m2+\frac14\left(n-\frac{\Phi_k(G)}k\right)
=\frac m2+\frac{m}{2k}
=\frac{k+1}{2k}\,m.
\]
This proves the odd case. If $k$ is even, apply the odd case with
$k+1$, using $\Delta(G)\le k+1$, to obtain
$\operatorname{bis}(G)\ge\frac{k+2}{2(k+1)}m$.

Finally, $K_{k+1}$ has $k(k+1)/2$ edges, and every bisection of it
has $\left\lfloor (k+1)^2/4\right\rfloor$ crossing edges. Consequently,
\[
\frac{\operatorname{bis}(K_{k+1})}{|E(K_{k+1})|}
=\frac{\left\lfloor (k+1)^2/4\right\rfloor}{k(k+1)/2}
=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{k+1}{2k},&\text{if $k$ is odd},\\[6pt]
\displaystyle\frac{k+2}{2(k+1)},&\text{if $k$ is even}.
\end{cases}
\]
Both coefficients are therefore best possible.
